Huygens Pyth

GeometryAreaTriangles
Game: This picture shows why the square on the longest side of a right-angled triangle is exactly the same size as the two other squares together. There is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the three round points to change the shape, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick names or hint to see more, and press Reset to go back to the start.

Look for the math

Christiaan Huygens published this proof in 1657. It takes the three squares on a right triangle and cuts the largest one into two strips. Each strip has half the area of one of the smaller squares, so the two together are exactly the large square.

A right triangle and its squares

Point C always stays at a right angle: moving C slides it round the circle through A and B, and moving A or B rebuilds C at the same angle. Write a = BC, b = AC and c = AB. The Pythagorean theorem says a² + b² = c². The readout above checks it on every shape you make; the logic test checked it on a grid and on 600 random triangles.

Halves that match

The proof extends GA to P with AP = AG = AC, and BD to N with BN = BD = BC. Triangle ABP has half the area of the square on AC, and triangle ANB has half the area of the square on BC. Triangle APS has the same three sides as ABC, which gives PS = BC = BN; triangle KPS then has the same sides as ANB, so it too is half the square on BC. Tick hint to see those halves shaded. Two lines on the original page have slips: it says AP = AD = AC, but D sits on the other square and AD is not AC — the letter should be G. It also writes ∠KPS where the equal angle is ∠KSP.

Two strips fill the big square

Euclid I.41 says a parallelogram and a triangle on the same base and between the same parallels have areas in the ratio two to one. So strip ABML is twice triangle ABP, and strip KMLS is twice triangle KPS. Their areas are AC² and BC², and together they fill the square on AB. The page calls the strips rectangles; once you turn AB they are slanted parallelograms, which is exactly what Euclid's rule covers. The area argument still works.

Tick names to find G and D, then drag C so that P or N lands near a corner of the drawing.
